clue.text: Fish part of the canal with weed in it

parts.note: the char is a trout-like freshwater fish
a lock is the gated section of a canal where boats are raised or lowered

explanation.surface: An angler notices a fish in a weedy stretch of canal.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'with weed in it' as a description of the canal; 'weed' is the definition and 'with ... in it' merely links.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlock is wild mustard, a yellow-flowered plant counted as a field weed.

clue.text: Daily work of soldiers ?

definitions.meaning: a regular newspaper article by one writer
a formation of troops marching in a long file

explanation.definitionFit: A journalist writes a regular newspaper column, and a column of troops is a marching file.

clue.text: Coming for a few weeks ?

definitions.meaning: the church season of about four weeks before Christmas

explanation.definitionFit: Advent means an arrival, and it is also the four-week church season before Christmas.

clue.text: Also fills new places in the picture

indicators.note: the word for also fills the gap in the middle of the rearranged letters
new places means the letters of places made into a new order

parts.note: and means also, in addition

explanation.surface: Someone also fills new spaces in a painting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'picture' tempts as a verb; it is the definition, and 'fills' means the word for also is placed inside the rearranged letters, not wrapped round them.
explanation.definitionFit: A landscape is a painting or picture of rural scenery.

clue.text: Biscuit of rarer make — three hundred varieties

indicators.note: varieties of the letters means different arrangements of them

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, so three hundred is CCC

explanation.surface: A biscuit comes in three hundred varieties, each rarer than the last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'varieties' scrambles RARERMAKE together with CCC.
explanation.definitionFit: A cream cracker is a crisp, unsweetened British biscuit usually eaten with cheese.

clue.text: Renounce American father wanting return of cat

parts.note: Pa is an informal word for father, common in American speech

indicators.note: the return of a word means it is read backwards, right to left

parts.note: puss is a familiar word for a cat

explanation.surface: Someone gives something up because a father misses the homecoming of the family cat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wanting' looks like a deletion signal but only links; 'Pa' for father is the American-flavoured word.
explanation.definitionFit: To pass up an offer is to decline or forgo it, a phrasal-verb synonym.

clue.text: Prince's breathless adsum "is heard ?

definitions.note: Prince's reads as Prince is, the 's linking definition to wordplay

indicators.note: the dropped-aitch phrase is said out loud and gives the sound of the entry

parts.note: adsum is the Latin roll-call reply meaning I am here; said breathlessly, the h dropped, it becomes am 'ere

explanation.surface: A breathless prince answers the school register.
explanation.walkthrough: Adsum, 'I am here' in Latin, is a pupil's answer to the roll; 'breathless' drops the H, and 'am 'ere' said aloud gives the Eastern title.
explanation.definitionFit: Ameer is a variant of emir, a Muslim prince or ruler.

clue.text: Woman secures about fifty ponies

indicators.note: the joined pieces go about the next letter, around it

parts.note: she is the pronoun for a woman
ties means fastens or secures
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A woman fastens around fifty ponies together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'secures' is the second piece of a charade, not a container signal; it is 'about' that puts the Roman fifty between the woman and the fastening.
explanation.definitionFit: Shelties is a familiar name for Shetland ponies (or sheepdogs).

clue.text: Just heaven when one's in the show!

indicators.note: the next pieces go in the middle of the show

parts.note: a parade is a public procession or show
one is the numeral I, and 's is S

explanation.surface: Being a performer in a show is simply blissful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one's' is I + S, placed in PARADE before its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that is simply heaven, sheer bliss, is paradise.

clue.text: He's off like the wind

parts.note: 'He's off' reads as someone who has bolted; the wind is the levanter, an easterly wind of the Mediterranean whose name shares the verb's root

explanation.surface: A runner sprints away at great speed.
explanation.walkthrough: To levant is an old word for absconding, especially to dodge debts; the levanter is an east wind, so the absconder goes off 'like the wind' in two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Levant means abscond, so someone who has levanted has run off, here with a nod to the levanter wind.

clue.text: Space traveller of Gloster

definitions.meaning: a shooting star streaking through space and burning up in the sky
the Gloster aircraft company built a famous early British jet fighter of this name

explanation.surface: A rocket or spaceship built by an aircraft firm.
explanation.walkthrough: Gloster was a British aircraft maker; its jet fighter of the 1940s carried this name.
explanation.definitionFit: A shooting star travels through space, and the same name was given to the Gloster jet fighter.

clue.text: Article about Maryland leader in Congress upset alarmists

indicators.note: the three small pieces sit in the middle of the rearranged letters
Congress upset means its letters are knocked into a new order

parts.note: a is the indefinite article
re is Latin for about, concerning

indicators.note: the leader of Maryland is the first letter of that state's name

explanation.surface: A story about Maryland's leader causes uproar in Congress.
explanation.walkthrough: A, RE and M go in SCONGERS, the anagram of CONGRESS from 'upset'.
explanation.definitionFit: Scaremongers spread alarming rumours, as alarmists do.

clue.text: Less dash ?

definitions.meaning: the short horizontal stroke used as the subtraction sign

explanation.definitionFit: Minus means less in arithmetic, and the minus sign is a short dash.

clue.text: Staff gets reproved-is mortified

parts.note: a mace is a ceremonial staff of office
to rate someone is an old word for scolding them

explanation.surface: An official carrying a staff of office is told off and feels deeply embarrassed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mortified' is used in its older religious sense, the flesh subdued by fasting, not 'embarrassed'; to rate is an old verb for scold.
explanation.definitionFit: Macerated once meant wasted away by fasting, the ascetic sense of mortified flesh.

clue.text: Head attendants put locks on furniture

parts.note: locks are tresses of hair
dressers are pieces of furniture, sideboards with shelves

explanation.surface: Servants are told to put padlocks on the household furniture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head attendants' suggests senior servants; it means those who attend to heads.
explanation.definitionFit: Barbers and stylists look after people's heads, so they are attendants of the head.

clue.text: Dispatched something about people giving opinion

parts.note: sent means dispatched

indicators.note: the word for something goes about the people, around them

parts.note: it can stand for a thing, something
men as people in general

explanation.surface: Something is sent out to collect people's opinions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' wraps the word for something round the people, not the dispatched word round anything; 'giving' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: A sentiment is a view or feeling held on a matter.

clue.text: Under acute stress?

parts.note: read as a letter with an acute mark written on it, or a syllable bearing stress

explanation.surface: Someone is suffering severe stress.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about anxiety; the reading is a vowel marked with an acute accent, or a stressed syllable.
explanation.definitionFit: A letter under an acute mark carries an accent, and a syllable given stress is emphasised.

clue.text: Can I include a hundred as friendly?

indicators.note: the question's letters include the hundred, which goes inside them

parts.note: can I is the question am I able
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether they may count a hundred as friends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can I' becomes AM I ABLE, run together; 'include' puts C in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Amicable means showing goodwill, the way friends behave.

clue.text: Gives us a longer start

parts.note: a word that means start but uses many more letters than the five of 'start'

explanation.surface: A race official grants competitors a bigger head start.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about a handicap in a race; the cryptic reading is that the answer is simply a much longer word meaning beginning.
explanation.definitionFit: Commencement is a formal, lengthier synonym of the beginning of something.

clue.text: Mind about returning to the course?

parts.note: to care is to mind or be concerned

indicators.note: returning means the short word for about is read backwards

parts.note: re is Latin for about, concerning

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether to go back to the racecourse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' is a reversal of the word for about, and 'to' merely links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A career is a person's course through working life.

clue.text: It might be nice to be intellectual

indicators.note: it might be nice to be something else, so those letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone thinks it would be pleasant to be clever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It might be' rearranges the letters of NICE TO.
explanation.definitionFit: Noetic means relating to the mind or intellect.

clue.text: Uncle may be without the idea of a mathematician

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the rearranged letters surround the next piece
Uncle may be something else, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An uncle is said to have no grasp of a mathematician's thinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' means outside, not lacking: the anagram of the uncle (from 'may be') goes round the idea. 'the' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Euclidean describes the geometry of Euclid, the ancient Greek mathematician.

clue.text: Perfect declaration of card player ?

definitions.meaning: the dealer announcing whose turn it is to hand out the cards

explanation.definitionFit: Ideal means flawless, and read as 'I deal' it is what the dealer at cards says.

clue.text: I am having a shot at a butterfly

parts.note: I am contracts to I'm
a go is a try or attempt, a shot at something

explanation.surface: A collector says he is going to try to net a butterfly.
explanation.definitionFit: An imago is the final adult stage of an insect, such as a butterfly emerged from its chrysalis.

clue.text: Log furniture ?

definitions.meaning: printed lists of logarithms used for calculation

explanation.definitionFit: Log tables are mathematical reference lists, and tables are also everyday pieces of furniture.

clue.text: Building people break principle

indicators.note: the men break into the principle, splitting its letters apart

parts.note: a tenet is a principle or belief
men as people in general

explanation.surface: Constructing something means some people abandon their principles.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenement is a large building divided into flats.

clue.text: Abides by arrangement of dunderhead novelist

parts.note: the head of 'dunder', its first letter; the word is split, as hyphenated across the printed line, into dunder and head
H. G. Wells, English novelist of The War of the Worlds

explanation.surface: Someone puts up with a novelist arranged by a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dunder-head' is printed hyphenated: the head of 'dunder' gives its first letter. 'by arrangement of' only links, not an anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: To dwell is to live or stay somewhere, as abides does.

clue.text: Secret ? One secret ? Nothing of the sort!

indicators.note: 'nothing of the sort' is read as letters made into a different sort, rearranged

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: Asked if something is secret, a speaker hotly denies it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nothing of the sort!' reads as a denial, but 'Nothing' is O and 'of the sort' rearranges I, SECRET and O.
explanation.definitionFit: Esoteric knowledge is known only to an inner circle, hence private or hidden.
